one_liner: D toolkit of single-purpose TSV tools (filter, select, join, summarize) that outruns awk, cut and datamash on multi-GB files.
what_it_does: Twelve standalone Unix-style executables for tab-delimited data: tsv-filter (numeric, string and regex tests per field), tsv-select (cut with named fields, reordering and exclusion), tsv-join, tsv-summarize, tsv-uniq, tsv-sample, tsv-split, tsv-append, tsv-pretty, csv2tsv, number-lines and keep-header. Each reads files or stdin and writes stdout, is header-aware (-H) and addresses fields by number or name. It replaces awk one-liners, cut and datamash with dedicated flags rather than a scripting language.
how_it_is_fast: Input goes through bufferedByLine, which rawReads 128 KB blocks and hands out line slices in place instead of copying each line; output goes through BufferedOutputRange, which batches writes into about 10 KB chunks before touching stdout (the author says output buffering gave the biggest gain on the narrow-line test). tsv-filter splits only up to the highest field a test references and runs a precompiled list of test closures; tsv-select uses InputFieldReordering plus template specialisation to drop branches from the inner loop. Prebuilt binaries are LDC builds with -O3 -boundscheck=off plus PGO and LTO extended into druntime and Phobos; the 2018 page lists LTO/PGO, output buffering and compiler improvements as the sources of the 7-64% gain over 2017. Everything is single-threaded.
when_to_use: Repeated filtering, column selection, joins or per-column statistics over plain TSV files in the hundreds of MB to tens of GB on one machine, where awk or datamash pipelines are the bottleneck.
Pipelines where field names in the header are easier to maintain than awk field numbers ($4, $16).
Numeric row filters and summary statistics, where the 2018 Linux run shows about 2x over mawk 1.3.3, 7.8x over GNU awk and 3.1x over GNU Datamash.
Converting messy CSV once (csv2tsv) and then working in escape-free TSV with the rest of the toolkit.
x86-64 Linux or macOS hosts where the prebuilt LTO+PGO binaries can be dropped onto PATH.
when_not_to_use: Short lines or small files: GNU cut beat tsv-select on the 86M-line narrow test on Linux (5.60 vs 8.26 s) and on a 279 MB file in the 2017 study (0.99 vs 1.21 s).
Pure column cutting where a newer specialist is available: hck (1.198 s) and tuc are faster than tsv-select (1.702 s) in hck's own run on the same file.
Regex filtering, where xsv (Rust) was faster on both platforms in 2018 (7.97 vs 8.80 s Linux, 7.03 vs 8.28 s macOS).
Real CSV with quoted delimiters or embedded newlines in every step: only csv2tsv understands CSV escapes; the other tools split blindly on the delimiter.
Arbitrary per-row logic (computed columns, conditionals across many fields): there is no expression language, so awk or Miller remain necessary.

integration.form: standalone executables (prebuilt tarballs, make, or dub)
integration.dependencies: none at run time (prebuilt Linux binaries statically link the C runtime); building needs a D compiler (DMD 2.088.1+ or LDC 1.18.0+; LDC 1.9.0+ for LTO/PGO)
integration.min_toolchain: LDC 1.18.0 or DMD 2.088.1 (prebuilt v2.2.0 uses LDC 1.24.0); builds with current compilers are not documented
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS, x86-64 prebuilt only; no ARM64 assets (issue #357), v2.2.1 has no Linux assets (issue #349); Windows only via WSL or Docker (issue #317)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — new command-line syntax (tsv-filter --gt 4:0.3, tsv-select -f 1,8,19); tsv-select covers cut -f usage, the others replace specific awk or datamash idioms rather than accepting their scripts

gotchas: Stricter than awk: tsv-filter aborts with 'Not enough fields in line' on short or blank lines (open issue #355 was trailing blank lines), throws when a numeric test hits a non-numeric field instead of treating it as 0, and the tools reject CRLF line endings.

Speed depends on the build: source builds default to DMD without LTO/PGO, and the 2017 study shows DMD up to 2x slower than LDC (tsv-join 41.23 vs 20.78 s, csv2tsv 56.08 vs 27.41 s); use make DCOMPILER=ldc2 LDC_LTO_RUNTIME=1 LDC_PGO=2 or the prebuilt binaries.
Release builds use -release -boundscheck=off, so D's array bounds checks and asserts are off in the shipped binaries.

Benchmark harness gaps: the Linux mawk baseline is 1.3.3 while macOS used 1.3.4, locale is not stated (it affects GNU awk regex and field handling but not cut), C tools come from package managers with unstated flags, Datamash was fed through 'cat |', and no output-equivalence check is described.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tsv-utils over hck or tuc when you need filtering, joins, sampling and statistics in one consistent header-aware toolkit, not only column cutting, where hck and tuc are faster; pick it over Miller 6 or awkrs when the job is a fixed filter or summary on large TSV and a scripting language is not needed.
verified_claims_summary: In the April 2018 first-party study (v1.1.19 LTO+PGO binaries vs package-manager C tools, 10th percentile of 35 runs on a 16-CPU Haswell 2095 MHz Ubuntu 16.04 cloud VM), tsv-filter took 5.48 s vs mawk 1.3.3 11.31 s and GNU awk 4.2.1 42.80 s on a 4.8 GB numeric filter, tsv-select 4.79 s vs GNU cut 8.25 14.46 s, and tsv-summarize 15.78 s vs Datamash 1.3 48.51 s, while GNU cut won the narrow-line test and xsv the regex test. An independent hyperfine run in the hck README (Ryzen 9 3950X, Ubuntu 20) measured tsv-select v2.2.0 at 1.702 s vs GNU cut 8.30 at 7.541 s (min 6.827 s) and awk at 4.993 s on the 7M-line HEPMASS CSV.
status_note: Effectively unmaintained since the v2.2.1 tag of 2021-06-13 (21 open issues, unanswered requests for Linux and ARM64 binaries) but BSL-1.0, not archived, and the x86-64 v2.2.0 binaries still work as standalone executables.
